extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, literary critics, and students of English literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical standards for writing and judging poetry and literary prose, emphasising plainness, word-choice, pruning of ornament, and methods of critical training and biographical testimony. Focused on 19th-century English poetic practice but broadly applicable to poetic composition and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obscurity and turgid diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics objected to obscurity, a general turgidness of diction, and a profusion of new coined double epithets in youthful poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author admits the charge, pruned double epithets in later editions, and sought to 'tame the swell and glitter both of thought and diction.' The rule is to avoid unnecessarily obscure or inflated wording; revise and simplify where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for admission of double epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule for the admission of double epithets seems to be: either that they should be already denizens of our language (e.g., 'blood-stained', 'terror-stricken'), or, when a new epithet is hazarded, that it at least be one word, not two words made one by printer's hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inventing epithets, prefer single-word coinages to hyphenated two-word compounds; prefer commonly established compounds. If a compounded idea can be better expressed in simpler terms, seek another mode of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer austere, natural style over ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: An austere and more natural style is superior to excessive ornament; the author reverenced those who re-introduced manly simplicity of the Greek and elder English poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study simpler, native diction (Homer, elder English poets) and aim to impress naturalness on compositions. Avoid ornament for its own sake; cultivate simplicity informed by disciplined judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid grandiloquence translatable into simpler words
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever is translatable in other and simpler words of the same language, without loss of sense or dignity, is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a phrase can be rendered in plainer language without losing sense or dignity, prefer the plainer phrasing. 'Dignity' here denotes absence of ludicrous or debasing associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every word and word-position must be justified
rubrics_metrics.description: In truly great poets there is a reason assignable not only for every word, but for the position of every word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or editing, examine synonyms and positions; show why a particular word or placement is necessary. Precision and intentionality in word-choice are essential to good poetic diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overused similes, introductions and stock examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain introductions, similes, and examples (e.g., the repeated use of 'Alexander and Clytus') are to be interdicted as overused and trite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a mental or explicit list of worn-out phrases and images to avoid. Substitute fresher or more apt examples; restrain reliance on the few 'serviceable' similes that become clichés.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical training: rigorous redrafting and fault intolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: Teacher's practice: accumulate student exercises, question placements of sentences, and if repeated faults appear (two faults of same kind), tear up the exercise and require a new one on the same subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use disciplined, exacting exercises and forced redrafting to correct recurring faults. Encourage students to defend placement/wording, and require rework when explanations are unsatisfactory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the authority of great models instructively
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority of Milton and Shakespeare may be usefully pointed out to young authors; compare early vs. mature works to learn economy of diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study canonical models (e.g., Milton's earlier and later works) to observe development toward fewer double epithets and greater clarity; use examples from the masters as teaching exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prune youthful ornament carefully but not destructively
rubrics_metrics.description: Youthful 'parasite' ornament (double epithets, glitter) should be pruned vigorously, but sometimes ornaments are entwined with a poem and disentangling them risks damaging the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit aggressively for excess ornament, but be cautious when excising material tightly integrated into the poem; balance pruning with preservation of the poem's integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: English is unfitted for excessive compounds; prefer other expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: A language which, like the English, is almost without cases, is in its very genius unfitted for compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of forming many compounds, seek other ways of expressing the same sense (simpler words, rephrasing). Overreliance on compound coinages is discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biographical evidence should balance friends and enemies
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary biography can only proceed from friends, enemies, or indifferent persons; the testimony of friends is needed to balance that of adversaries and gives the best grounds for judging a man's character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing biography, solicit and include friends' testimony to counterbalance hostile accounts; recognize limits of indifferent observers who often know little. Consider multiple perspectives but value close, long acquaintance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest about partialities in biographical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The author did not strive to conceal natural partialities; he believes reporters should be honest and say only what they really think and feel, so that their colour will not finally obscure the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A biographer should be transparent about personal biases rather than pretending neutrality; candidness about partiality helps readers weigh testimony and safeguards overall truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish principles from manifestations in moral/critical judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles cannot go too far (they are boundless), but manifestations (thoughts, words, deeds) are limited and may exceed in degree even if they correspond to what is right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In moral and critical assessment, differentiate abstract principles from concrete expressions; judge the form/mode of manifestation (excess, rashness) rather than condemning principle itself.
